hook.text: A single chicken farm can house a million birds. They never see sunlight or touch the ground.

buildup.text: After World War II, animal farming industrialized. Confinement operations maximized output per square foot.

discovery.text: Factory farming cut meat prices dramatically. Chicken went from a luxury to the cheapest protein available.

twist.text: Concentrated animal waste pollutes waterways. Antibiotic overuse breeds resistant superbugs.

climax.text: Factory farms produce 75% of the world's poultry and 40% of pork. Scale drives the entire system.

punchline.text: Cheap meat comes with hidden costs.

quiz.question: What percentage of the world's poultry comes from factory farms?

details.summary: Factory farming, or intensive animal agriculture, raises livestock at industrial scale in confined facilities to maximize output and minimize cost. This topic covers its post-WWII rise, efficiency gains, and the ethical, environmental, and health concerns it generates.
details.whyItMatters: Factory farming produces most of the world's meat, eggs, and dairy at prices consumers expect, but at significant costs to animal welfare, the environment, and public health that are increasingly hard to ignore.
takeaways: Factory farms produce over 70% of the world's poultry and over 40% of its pork
Concentrated animal operations generate massive waste and pollution problems
Routine antibiotic use in factory farms contributes to antimicrobial resistance

faq.question: What is factory farming and when did it start?
faq.answer: Factory farming is large-scale, industrial production of livestock in confined facilities designed for maximum efficiency. It emerged after World War II as cheap grain, antibiotics, and new breeds enabled dense confinement of poultry, pigs, and cattle.

faq.question: What are the main criticisms of factory farming?
faq.answer: Critics highlight animal welfare concerns from extreme confinement, pollution from concentrated waste, antibiotic overuse driving resistance, worker safety issues, displacement of small farmers, and the large climate footprint from methane and manure.
